summary: Comments on the Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing Telnet option described in RFC 560. It restates that the option lets the server control, on the user-to-server path, when characters are echoed and when they are sent, and then offers critique of the design.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone read the plan for letting a far computer control typing echo and wrote down what he thought was good and what could be better.

subtitle: Technical critique of the RCTE Telnet option for controlling character echoing and transmission.

tldr.problem: RFC 560 describes RCTE (Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing), which lets a server control when characters are echoed and sent on a Telnet user connection.
tldr.mechanism: RCTE uses server commands to set which characters trigger transmission. But the author argues it requires users to wait for server responses before transmitting their next character, eliminating the efficiency gain it aims for.
tldr.outcome: The author proposes an alternative: users should transmit based on their current understanding of the transmission character set, not wait for confirmation from the server.

facts.label: Core issue
facts.value: Transmission character set changes and timing

today: RFC 563 is a technical commentary on a specific Telnet option that was never widely adopted. Modern terminal emulation and network speeds have largely made these low-level optimizations obsolete.

sections.title: Why Echo and Transmission Control Matter
sections.content:
Telnet users at satellite-linked sites experience noticeable latency—the delay between pressing a key and seeing it echoed on screen is distracting. RFC 357 proposed Remote Controlled Echoing (RCE) to fix this: the server echoes characters immediately at the server, reducing perceived delay.

Later, RFC 560 added transmission control: the server specifies which characters should trigger a packet transmission from the user to the server. Character-by-character transmission wastes bandwidth and processing. Buffering characters until the end of a command, then transmitting the whole command, is more efficient.
sections.plainLanguage: When you type at a computer far away, you see your keystrokes after a delay. RCTE tries to fix this and also save bandwidth by letting the far computer say which typed characters trigger a send.

sections.title: The Problem With RCTE's Approach
sections.content:
The author's main complaint: RCTE makes the user wait. When a user types characters, the server may later change which characters trigger transmission. During the time it takes for that change to arrive, the user's local system does not know the new transmission rules.

RCTE, as described in the example with TENEX, would have the user hold all characters until the server confirms the new transmission character set. This restores the round-trip delay penalty—a human must wait for the server's response before typing can proceed. Yet RCTE's goal was to eliminate exactly that penalty.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says "send when you see a carriage return." The user types several lines while waiting for the server's response. If the server changes the rule, the user might not know yet. RCTE makes the user wait to be sure.

sections.title: An Alternative Strategy
sections.content:
The author proposes that users transmit based on the transmission character set in effect at the moment of typing. If the server later changes the rules, the user may briefly send incomplete commands or extra characters, but the penalty is small: improved channel use and the ability to overlap I/O and computation.

The author illustrates with examples involving TENEX interactions and two users linked through a TENEX, showing cases where RCTE would cause unnecessary delays.
sections.plainLanguage: Just send when you think you should, based on what you last heard from the server. It might not be perfect, but it keeps you from waiting for confirmation every time.
